**Options documented under `[tool.ruff.format]`:**
- `quote-style`: preferred quote character, `double` (default), `single` or `preserve`.
- `indent-style`: indent with spaces (default) or tabs.
- `skip-magic-trailing-comma`: when `true`, ignores trailing commas as a signal to keep multi-line formatting (default `false`).
- `line-ending`: `auto` (default), `lf`, `cr-lf` or `native`.
- `docstring-code-format`: reformat Python code examples inside docstrings (default `false`).
- `docstring-code-line-length`: line length for those docstring examples, either `"dynamic"` (default, follows the global line length) or a fixed integer.
- `nested-string-quote-style`: quote style for nested strings in f-string expressions, `alternating` (default) or `preferred`. It only applies to Python 3.12+.
- `exclude`: extra file patterns to leave out of formatting, on top of the global exclusions.
- `preview`: turn on the unstable preview formatting style (default `false`).

**Related settings the formatter pages mention:**
- `line-length`: the maximum line width. It is a top-level `[tool.ruff]` setting, not a format option.
- `extension`: maps custom file extensions, such as `mdx` and `qmd`, to Markdown formatting.
- `extend-exclude`: used to exclude Markdown files from formatting.
- `--check` (`ruff format --check`): reports unformatted files without writing changes.
- `--exit-non-zero-on-format`: exits with status 1 when files were formatted.

8. **[CORS](https://hono.dev/docs/middleware/builtin/cors)** sets Cross-Origin Resource Sharing headers and handles preflight requests.

10. **[ETag](https://hono.dev/docs/middleware/builtin/etag)** adds `ETag` headers to responses and returns 304 Not Modified when the client's copy is current.

Yes, several people have. These are the ones I'd start with. I only have the search results, not the full pages, so I haven't checked how thorough each one is.

**Best for benchmark numbers**
- [Research and analysis of performance of LLM on the Raspberry Pi 5](https://stratospherelinuxips.readthedocs.io/en/develop/immune/research_rpi_llm_performance.html) (Stratosphere Lab). It measured Llama 3.2 1B (Q4_K_M) at about 11.2 tokens/s and Llama 3.2 3B at about 4.7 tokens/s. It used Ollama.
- [Ollama vs llama.cpp on Raspberry Pi 5](https://medium.com/@omkar121212/ollama-vs-llama-cpp-on-raspberry-pi-5-8e7fbeb310de) (Medium). It compares the two runtimes on TinyLlama 1.1B. llama.cpp was slightly faster at generation, at about 14.4 tokens/s.

**Best for step-by-step setup**
- [Arm Learning Path: Llama 3 on Raspberry Pi 5](https://learn.arm.com/learning-paths/embedded-and-microcontrollers/rpi-llama3/) (Arm). It runs Llama 3 with ExecuTorch rather than Ollama. You need a Meta license request to download the model, and the download link is valid for 24 hours.
- [Run Llama3-8b on a Raspberry Pi 5 with ExecuTorch](https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/run-llama3-8b-on-a-raspberry-pi-5-with-executorch/2048) (PyTorch forum). It reports about 2 tokens/s for the 8B model.
- [Raspberry Pi Ollama](https://pimylifeup.com/raspberry-pi-ollama/) (Pi My Life Up) is a simple Ollama walkthrough.

**Other options**
- [Running a ChatGPT-like LLM on the Raspberry Pi 5](https://www.hackster.io/shahizat/running-a-chatgpt-like-llm-on-the-raspberry-pi-5-fd67f9) (Hackster) runs a 7B model with llama.cpp at about 2 tokens/s.
- [Run LLMs on Raspberry Pi 5](https://tinyweights.dev/posts/run-llms-raspberry-pi-5/) (tinyweights.dev). It expects 5–15 tokens/s for 1.5B models and 2–5 tokens/s for 3B. Its memory-bandwidth figures contradict each other (17 GB/s in one place, 34 GB/s in another), so I'd treat its numbers with some caution.

**What the write-ups agree on**
- The 8 GB Pi 5 is the usual recommendation.
- 1B–3B models at 4-bit quantization are the practical range, at roughly 5–15 tokens/s.
- 7B–8B models run at about 2 tokens/s.
- Generation speed is limited by memory bandwidth, so smaller quantized models are much faster.

I didn't find a dedicated Ollama benchmark of Llama 3 8B on the Pi 5. If you need that number, run `ollama run --verbose` or `llama-bench` yourself.

** For static apps, set the Artifact Folder to `dist`. For SSR, set the Entry Point to `entry.mjs` and the Artifact Folder to `dist/server`.
- **Clever Cloud:** The app must listen on port 8080. The guide's start script is `node ./dist/server/entry.mjs --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080`.
- **Cloudflare:** If you see a "Hydration completed but contains mismatches" error, turn off Auto Minify.
- **Deno Deploy:** SSR needs `@deno/astro-adapter`. Static sites need no extra configuration.
- **EdgeOne Pages:** You can deploy from a Git connection or with the EdgeOne CLI.
- **Firebase:** Static sites need no extra configuration. SSR needs the Node adapter and a Blaze plan or higher.
- **Fly.io:** `fly launch` detects Astro, builds the image and deploys. SSR needs the Node adapter first.
- **Google Cloud:** For a static site on Cloud Storage, give `allUsers` the Storage Object Viewer role. Set `index.html` as the entrypoint and `404.html` as the error page.
- **Hostinger:** Build locally and upload `dist/` to `public_html` through hPanel's File Manager or FTP.

This was an 8-week trial in resistance-trained men comparing 16:8 TRE with a normal diet. Fat mass dropped and lean mass was maintained. The sample was small and the participants were trained, so the result is encouraging but limited.

**3. Liu et al., 2022, *New England Journal of Medicine*.**
This was a 12-month RCT in adults with obesity. It compared TRE plus calorie restriction with calorie restriction alone. Weight loss was similar in both arms, and so were changes in lean mass. The result suggests the calorie deficit drives muscle loss more than the eating window does.

**Overall.** Muscle loss seems to depend mainly on the size of the calorie deficit, protein intake and resistance training. Fasting windows add little by themselves. Any weight-loss diet tends to lose some lean mass, typically about 20–30% of the weight lost. Lean mass is usually measured by DXA, which can overstate muscle loss.

8. **[CORS](https://hono.dev/docs/middleware/builtin/cors)** sets Cross-Origin Resource Sharing headers and handles preflight requests.

sses.dataclass` adds validation to standard dataclasses, with support for config, `Field()` and validators. They aren't a full replacement for models: they lack model methods, so you use `TypeAdapter`, and they drop extra data from serialization.
- **Experimental Features:** Covers the pipeline API (`validate_as`, `transform`, `predicate`) and partial validation of incomplete data such as streamed LLM output. It also covers `generate_arguments_schema`. These features may change.
- **Fields:** Customizing fields with `Field()` or `Annotated`: defaults, aliases, constraints, strict mode, and frozen or excluded fields. It also covers deprecation, JSON Schema metadata and `@computed_field`.
- **Forward Annotations:** Lets models reference types defined later, using quoted annotations or `from __future__ import annotations` (Python 3.14+ defers evaluation). For cyclic imports, use `TYPE_CHECKING` blocks and `model_rebuild()`.
- **JSON:** Parsing with `model_validate_json` and `TypeAdapter.validate_json` uses the fast `jiter` parser. It also covers partial parsing of incomplete JSON and JSON serialization with `model_dump_json`.
- **JSON Schema:** Generates JSON Schema (Draft 2020-12, OpenAPI 3.1) from models and types in validation or serialization mode. You can customize it with `Field` options, `json_schema_extra`, `WithJsonSchema`, `SkipJsonSchema` or a custom `GenerateJsonSchema` subclass.
- **Models:** Models are classes inheriting from `BaseModel`, with type-annotated fields validated on instantiation. The page also covers validation and serialization methods, extra-data handling, nested and generic models, `RootModel` and immutability.
- **Performance tips:** Use `model_validate_json()`, create a `TypeAdapter` once, and prefer `list`/`dict` over `Sequence`/`Mapping`. Use tagged unions, avoid wrap validators and nested models, and use `FailFast` to stop at the first sequence error.
- **Settings Management:** `pydantic-settings` is a companion package. `BaseSettings` loads validated config from environment variables, `.env` files, secrets files and cloud secret stores, and it also covers CLI parsing and source priority. This page is very long, so I only read the first ~100k of its ~127k characters.
- **Serialization:** `model_dump()` and `model_dump_json()` turn models into dicts or JSON. You can customize output with plain or wrap serializers and control inclusion with `exclude`, `include`, `exclude_unset` and `exclude_none`.
- **Strict Mode:** Makes validation reject values it would otherwise coerce, such as `'123'` for an `int` field. You can enable it per call, per field or model-wide.
- **Type Adapter:** `TypeAdapter` validates, serializes and generates schemas for non-`BaseModel` types such as `list[Model]`, TypedDicts and primitives. Create it once and reuse it, and use `defer_build` for forward references.
- **Types:** Covers built-in, standard library and extra types, plus utilities like `OnErrorOmit` and `FailFast`. It also explains custom types via `Annotated`, type aliases and `__get_pydantic_core_schema__`.
- **Unions:** Unions validate left-to-right, in smart mode (the default, which picks the best match) or as discriminated unions. The docs recommend discriminated unions for speed and predictability.
- **Validation Decorator:** `@validate_call` validates and coerces a function's arguments against its annotations before the function runs. It supports all parameter kinds, `Field()` constraints, aliases, async functions and custom config.
- **Validators:** Custom checks and transformations at field and model level, in after, before, plain and wrap modes, via `Annotated` or decorators. They can enforce cross-field rules, take a validation context, and raise errors with `ValueError`, `AssertionError` or `PydanticCustomError`.

This is the abstract of "Attention Is All You Need", the paper that introduced the Transformer. In plain words, it says:

- **The problem:** The best translation models at the time used complicated recurrent or convolutional neural networks. They also used an "attention" mechanism to link the encoder and decoder.
- **The idea:** The authors propose the **Transformer**, a simpler design built only on attention. It has no recurrence and no convolutions.
- **Why it matters:** Because it doesn't process words one after another, it can be trained in parallel. That makes training much faster.
- **Results:**
  - On English-to-German translation (WMT 2014), it scored 28.4 BLEU. That beat the previous best results, including ensembles of models, by more than 2 BLEU.
  - On English-to-French, a single model set a new record of 41.8 BLEU. It trained for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of what earlier top models cost.
  - It also did well on English constituency parsing, with both large and small training sets. That suggests it works on tasks beyond translation.

Here are three papers. I'm citing them from memory, without a live search, so check the details against PubMed before you rely on them.

1. **Lowe et al., 2020, *JAMA Internal Medicine*. "Effects of Time-Restricted Eating on Weight Loss and Other Metabolic Parameters in Women and Men With Overweight and Obesity: The TREAT Randomized Clinical Trial."**
   - In this 12-week RCT, 16:8 eating caused no more weight loss than regular meals.
   - Lean mass fell in the 16:8 group, including appendicular (limb) lean mass.
   - This is the main cautionary result. It was a small, short trial, though, and it didn't control protein intake or resistance training.

2. **Liu et al., 2022, *New England Journal of Medicine*. "Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss."**
   - This 12-month RCT in adults with obesity compared time-restricted eating plus calorie restriction against calorie restriction alone.
   - Adding the eating window gave no extra fat loss.
   - Lean mass changes were similar in both groups, so the muscle loss tracked the calorie deficit, not the timing.

3. **Moro et al., 2016, *Journal of Translational Medicine*. "Effects of eight weeks of time-restricted feeding (16/8) on basal metabolism, maximal strength, body composition, inflammation, and cardiovascular risk factors in resistance-trained males."**
   - Fat mass dropped and lean mass and strength were maintained.
   - This suggests that resistance training with adequate protein protects muscle.
   - The sample was small and the participants were already trained, so it may not apply to most people.

**Overall picture:** Intermittent fasting doesn't seem to cause more muscle loss than ordinary dieting at the same calorie deficit. Any weight loss tends to cost some lean mass, roughly a quarter or more of the weight lost in some studies. Resistance training and enough protein are the main protective factors. Many trials are short, and lean mass is often measured with DXA. DXA counts water and other non-muscle tissue as lean mass, so it overstates muscle.

**Other hosts and platforms**
- **Azion:** The CLI doesn't run natively on Windows, so Windows users need WSL. `node:*` imports can break the build because Azion's runtime lacks them.
- **Buddy:** It is CI/CD only and doesn't host your site. Set the deploy action's source path to `dist`.
- **Cleavr:** For SSR, set the entry point to `entry.mjs` and the artifact folder to `dist/server`. Static sites use `dist`.
- **Clever Cloud:** Apps listen on port 8080, so the `start` script passes `--host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080`. Static sites set `CC_WEBROOT="/dist"`.
- **Cloudflare:** Auto Minify can cause "Hydration completed but contains mismatches" errors. The fix is to turn it off.
- **CloudRay:** It doesn't host anything. It runs a reusable Bash deploy script on your own servers through an agent.
- **Deno Deploy:** Automatic mode doesn't work because Astro needs a build step. Use GitHub Action mode instead.
- **DeployHQ:** Like Buddy and CloudRay, it doesn't host. It builds your project and pushes the output over SSH/SFTP, FTP or to cloud storage.
- **EdgeOne Pages:** You can deploy from a Git repo or with EdgeOne's CLI. The guide links an official Astro template.
- **Firebase:** SSR requires the Blaze (paid) plan or higher. Static sites need no extra setup.
- **Fleek:** It is a decentralized, edge-optimized network for static sites. Its UI auto-detects Astro.
- **Fly.io:** `fly launch` detects Astro and generates a Dockerfile and `fly.toml`. SSR needs the Node adapter.
- **GitHub Pages:** The official Astro GitHub Action detects your package manager from the lockfile, so commit one.
- **GitLab Pages:** It only serves a folder named `public`. Set `outDir: 'public'` and rename your source `public/` folder to `static/`.
- **Google Cloud (Cloud Run):** Services aren't public by default. Grant "Cloud Run Invoker" to `allUsers` to open one up.
- **Heroku:** The guide uses the deprecated `heroku-static-buildpack` and points to `heroku-buildpack-nginx` instead.
- **Hostinger:** Static sites only need the `dist/` contents uploaded to `public_html`. SSR needs the Node adapter and a Node.js plan.
- **is\*hosting:** For on-demand sites, PM2 runs `dist/server/entry.mjs` on localhost:4321 and Nginx proxies public traffic to it.
- **Microsoft Azure:** The wizard-generated GitHub Action assumes Node 14, which breaks the build. Add an `engines` field in `package.json` requiring Node 22.22.0 or later.
- **Netlify:** `npx astro add netlify` installs the adapter and edits your config in one step.
- **Railway:** Its default builder, Railpack, builds static Astro sites automatically. SSR with the Node adapter follows Railway's own Astro guide.
- **Render:** The publish directory is `dist` for static sites, but `dist/client` if any pages render on demand.
- **Seenode:** Web services need port 80. The config reads `PORT` and falls back to 80.
- **Sevalla:** For SSR, use the Node adapter in standalone mode with `server.host: true`. The guide says the host setting is required for containers.
- **Stormkit:** It runs `npm run build` by default, which you can override. You can import projects from GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket.
- **Surge:** Publishing is one command, `surge dist`. Add a domain to use a custom one, as in `surge dist yourdomain.com`.
- **Vercel:** Static sites need no configuration. `astro add vercel` sets up on-demand rendering.
- **Zeabur:** It auto-detects GitHub-imported Astro projects. SSR needs `@zeabur/astro-adapter` and a two-line config change.
- **Zephyr Cloud:** It hashes build outputs with SHA-256 and uploads only new or changed assets.
- **Zerops:** The SSR `start` script runs `node ./dist/server/entry.mjs`, with `HOST=0.0.0.0` and `PORT=3000`.

Four of these (Buddy, CloudRay, DeployHQ and, in practice, Cleavr) are deployment tools rather than hosts. The first three say outright that they don't host your site.

13. **Serialization**: Models serialize to dicts or JSON, with control over aliases and field inclusion or exclusion, and support custom field- and model-level serializers. Subclass fields are omitted by default unless you use polymorphic serialization or `SerializeAsAny`.

17. **Unions**: Unions validate in left-to-right, smart (the default), or discriminated mode. Discriminated unions are the recommended choice for speed and predictability, and `Tag` and custom errors give clearer failure messages.
18. **Validation Decorator**: `@validate_call` checks and coerces function arguments against their annotations, and supports all parameter kinds and async functions. Return values are only validated with `validate_return=True`.
19. **Validators**: Custom field- and model-level validators in after, before, plain, and wrap modes, applied via `Annotated` or decorators. They can access validated data, context, and mode.

In plain words:

- **The problem:** The best translation and text-generation models at the time were complicated neural networks. They used recurrent or convolutional layers arranged as an encoder and a decoder. The strongest ones also used an "attention" mechanism to connect the encoder and decoder.
- **The idea:** The authors propose a simpler design called the **Transformer**. It drops the recurrent and convolutional parts and uses only attention.
- **The results:**
  - It scored better on English-to-German and English-to-French translation benchmarks.
  - It trained faster, because its computations can run in parallel.
  - It also worked well on a different task, English constituency parsing (analyzing sentence structure), which suggests it generalizes.

Here are three papers. I'm citing them from memory and haven't looked them up, so check the details before relying on them.

1. **Lowe DA, et al. (2020). "Effects of Time-Restricted Eating on Weight Loss and Other Metabolic Parameters in Women and Men With Overweight and Obesity: The TREAT Randomized Clinical Trial."** *JAMA Internal Medicine.*
   - This 12-week RCT compared 16:8 time-restricted eating with regular eating habits.
   - It found no significant weight-loss advantage for time-restricted eating.
   - Lean mass fell in the time-restricted group, including appendicular (limb) lean mass. This is the main paper behind the "fasting costs you muscle" concern. The trial had no resistance training and didn't control protein intake.

2. **Moro T, et al. (2016). "Effects of eight weeks of time-restricted feeding (16/8) on basal metabolism, maximal strength, body composition, inflammation, and cardiovascular risk factors in resistance-trained males."** *Journal of Translational Medicine.*
   - This was a small study of resistance-trained men.
   - Fat mass fell, and lean mass and strength were maintained.
   - It suggests that lifting weights, with adequate protein, can offset the muscle-loss risk. The sample was small, and the groups' calorie and protein intakes may have differed.

3. **Tinsley GM, et al. (2019). "Time-restricted feeding plus resistance training in active females: a randomized trial."** *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition.*
   - This RCT in active women paired time-restricted feeding with resistance training.
   - It found no clear benefit over normal eating for lean mass or strength, though the time-restricted group ate less protein.
   - Together with Moro, it points to the same takeaway.

**Takeaway:** Any calorie deficit tends to cost some lean mass, and intermittent fasting doesn't appear to be worse than ordinary dieting in this respect. Without resistance training and enough protein, though, some muscle loss is likely (Lowe). With training, muscle is generally preserved (Moro, Tinsley). Be careful with this literature: the trials are short and small, and "lean mass" from DEXA scans includes water and organ tissue, not only muscle.
